html:
Denazification was the Allied effort after World War II to remove Nazi influence from German public life, the courts, schools, business and the press. It began in 1945 in the four occupation zones, such as the American zone.

The Americans made millions of Germans fill in a questionnaire and sorted them into five groups, from major offenders to those cleared. The system was slow and clumsy. Most people ended as followers or were cleared, and many got certificates that were nicknamed "Persil notes", after a washing powder. The Nuremberg trials dealt with the top leaders only.

As the Cold War grew, the West wanted a stable Germany, and German-run panels took over the work. West Germany passed an amnesty in 1949 for lesser offences, and a law in 1951 let most dismissed civil servants back into service. Former Nazis returned to the courts, police, ministries and universities. Chancellor Konrad Adenauer argued the state needed their skills.

One result was that few prosecutors wanted to hunt war criminals. Fritz Bauer, a Jewish prosecutor in Hesse, did not trust the German authorities with the news that Eichmann had been found in Argentina, and sent it to Israel instead.
